title: Speech at Bellows Falls, Vermont
paragraphs: My fellow citizens, my fellow Americans, men and women of Vermont:

I have counted myself fortunate to be in Vermont and doubly fortunate to be here on Labor Day.(Cheers and applause) Labor Day is a typical American holiday(Cheers and applause), for the typical American is a man who works,(Cries of "That is so!) a man who works for himself, but who also knows how to work in combination with others.(Cheers and applause) And while I am very glad indeed to be greeted by all of you and thank you for the greeting, the rest will excuse my saying that I am particularly glad to be greeted by the representatives of organized labor.(Cheers and applause) This is in many ways a typical community. You have in this community representatives of the country and the city; that is you have the farmer, you have the wage-worker, you have the capitalist, all represented here and in the neighborhood, and gentlemen, it is in just such a neighborhood as this that we have a right to expect the development of those traits of character which we wish to think of as typically American. In the first place, in a small city, in a city where the town and country come close together it is more possible for men to realize what the government actually is than it [?] is possible to bring most men to realize in an enormous mass of people such [?] as you see in the great cities. Here it is brought home more to us [?] that the government is us. We are the government;(Cheers and applaus) you [?] and I, all of us. Now something can be done through government. We need [?] good laws and an honest administration of the law. We need laws which shall [?] secure fair play as between man and man, a square chance for a man to [?] win on his merits. As the social and economic conditions become more complex [?] there has to be an increase in the sphere of legislation. But there [?] is an enormous amount that law cannot do. A very, very great deal can [?] be done by association among ourselves— such associations as you see represented [?] here today— a [?]ssociations which will teach us [?] practically, in the best way that the lesson can be taught, by applying it, that not only must each work for himself, but that each must work for all; that we can accomplish by united self-help much, and that there yet remains an immense amount to be done by individual selfhelp in every association,

from the state, from the nation, to a union, to a corporation. We find that a man who is to accomplish good for his fellows must steadily endeavor not to be a passenger; he must pull his own weight and a little more.(Cheers and applause) There isn't any real place in our body politic for the idler. The law of healthy national life, and particularly so with us, is the law of work. If a man does his work well and it is honorable work, that is what we have a right to ask. Some work in one way and some in another, but as long as a man deals fairly with his neighbor, does not try to wrong him in any way, and as long as he works and it is work worth doing, he is a good citizen, and if he does not fulfill those attributes then he is a bad citizen.

As I say, each man must be able to work in conjunction with others, and he must also be able to work by himself. Every man of us at times stumbles; every man of us at times needs a helping hand; and shame to the man who when the need comes does not stretch out a helping hand to his brother(Applause). Every man stumbles and should then be helped. But if he lies down it is no use to carry him(Cheers and applause). He has got to try his best to walk, then help him on if you are worth anything; but if he lies down it is no use.(Applause)

There is no secret rule for good citizenship. I mean there is no specific, no patent for good citizenship. A man has got to have not only one quality, but several qualities, in order to make a good citizen, in order to make it worth our while to try to act with him. In the first place he has got to be honest, decent, fair in his dealings, and not just talk about it,— to be square in his dealings, and to begin at home. If a man isn't a good husband, a good father, he isn't a good citizen. It is a poor kind of creature who is always willing to reform the world but will not begin at home. He has got to be honest, and that is not enough. An honest man who is afraid is of mighty little good in the world. You have got to have courage with honesty. Honesty and courage— and those two are not enough. I do not care how honest and how brave a man is, if he is a natural born fool you can do nothing with him. To have the proper standard of citizenship we must have honesty, we must have courage, and we must have in addition the saving grace of common sense.(Applause)

No handwritten folio is visible on either Bellows Falls sheet (the tops are covered by the Chester sheet folded back), so both are given as "?". On page 1 (frame 0601) the left edge of the lower half of the text is hidden by the edge of an overlapping sheet, so the first one or two letters of about ten lines cannot be seen. Letters fully hidden are marked [illegible]; letters partly visible under the edge are marked .... No better image of this sheet was found on frames 0600-0603 (frame 0602 shows page 1 only upside down at the top, partly). A second look at the original or another filming would settle these. "is ax man": the letter after "a" is x-ed out on the typewriter. "realize xxxx": a typed word is x-ed out and cannot be read. "ix" (twice on p.1, once on p.2) is a typed "i" followed by an x-ed letter. "Labor Day" (second time): the "D" is typed over another letter. "particularly glad": the "g" is retraced by hand. "applaus)": the closing parenthesis is handwritten over the end of the word at the line end; a final "e" is not visible under it. "gentlemen,": a heavy hand stroke follows "gentlemen" with a handwritten comma after it; the stroke may cover a typed character. "ourselves,—": the typed comma is struck and a dash inserted by hand with a caret. "today— associations": a hand dash follows "today" and the first letter of "associations" is overwritten by hand (capital or lower case cannot be told). "teach us": the "u" is overtyped. The last typed line of page 1 is heavily struck through by hand; it appears to repeat the first line of page 2. "he must pull": "must" is written above with a caret; the caret's stroke runs through the "p" of "pull". "hand.;": a hand stroke turns the typed stop into a semicolon. "pàce": the second letter is two letters typed in one space. "fool": the first "o" is typed over another letter. "reform x": a typed x at the line end.
Third look, 2026-10-27: where the edge of the overlapping sheet hides the first letter or two of a word, the whole word is marked uncertain, as the word is clear from the visible letters.
